item.title: The "Baby Bag" Metaphor for Maternal Ambivalence
item.description:
Parenting

The "Baby Bag" Metaphor for Maternal Ambivalence

A podcast explores the emotional complexities of motherhood.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • Maternal ambivalence is about accepting conflicting emotions in motherhood.
  • The baby bag metaphor illustrates carrying diverse emotions in motherhood daily.
  • Safe spaces for moms help break taboos and normalize emotional transparency.

I was invited onto the “Beyond the Bump” podcast last month. This is an Australian podcast, hosted by two young mothers, Sophie Pearce and Jayde Couldwell, who have built up a large following in the maternal space. We had an amazing conversation about maternal ambivalence—it was authentic, curious, and energetic. We learnt about each other’s work and how they understand the everyday current experience of mothering. During our conversation, I had a glimpse into the workings of this passionate and enthusiastic team.

A Conversation About Maternal Ambivalence

We reflected on the everyday layered experiences of mothering and maternal ambivalence; how complicated mothering is and the importance of trying to make sense of it. These moms articulated the truths of their mothering so well, saying things like:

"The hard things are so often coupled with positive."

“Before having children, I’d never experienced something that made me feel so torn before."

"The reason we go back for more children is that yes, the hard parts are there, but there is beauty to it. It’s this delicate dance."

I chimed in, “And that's what ambivalence is. It's the ability to have two truths occurring at once."

We talked about how mothering is a continual process of making mistakes and repairing them, which is how we learn. This conversation led them back to their own childhood and to rethink what their own mothers went through. While they thought as children that their own mothers didn't make mistakes, they were able to revise this understanding. They recognized a symmetry between the generations and a newfound understanding that their mums also made many mistakes and often didn't know what they were doing. However, they remarked on a difference. Maybe in the old days, their mothers didn't have the freedom to voice their truth.

This recognition was one of many magic moments in our exchange. Mothers these days are becoming more comfortable talking about the challenges of mothering. Moms need a safe place to unpack their feelings, and those of us in the mothering space need to encourage this.

The enthusiastic conversation continued with other truths. As moms, we make it up as we go along; we need to remember that the vast majority of us do the best we can and that the difficulties of mothering are not there to be fixed but to learn from.

Then another moment of vulnerability entered into our exchange. It became evident that Sophie wasn't sure what maternal ambivalence really means.

I was thankful that they kept drilling me.

The Baby Bag Metaphor

Then there was a total pivot, an epiphany, a moment in conversation when Jayde began articulating her understanding of maternal ambivalence in the most sensitive and memorable way, using a metaphor of a baby bag.

I think we were all startled.

To paraphrase her words, she said that being a mom meant carrying a baby bag around all day. You can see through the bag that it contains many contradictory emotions, including frustration, anger, love, and sadness. She continued that every day your bag is full of these emotions. You carry it around, and then at the end of the day, once you sit back down and unpack the bag, you realize how necessary all this is. You do the same thing the next day, and you keep unpacking it. She cautioned that rather than stigmatizing these feelings, they need to be used.

What It Means to Have a Team

Aside from Jayde’s words, I was struck by the to-ing and fro-ing between these two women. I witnessed firsthand exactly what I mean when I talk about how crucial it is for a mum to have someone on her team: someone to both challenge and support her, someone who always has her back. I was faced with two mums who were building on the stories of their lives in honest conversation. It was so clear that they are each other’s team.

The co-hosts were encouraging and filling each other. As Jayde unpacked her metaphor, Sophie urged her on by saying, "Jayde, gorgeous, keep going," and "my G-d I’m gonna cry." She was saying: You reached me. They were speaking their own language—the strong and compassionate voice of two mothers together.

Then, more magic. Jayde added to her metaphor by saying, "Let's use these feelings to propel us to something more productive." Bullseye. This is maternal ambivalence. It's transformative. It’s what allows us to keep showing up every day. Their word propel is so powerful. I’m going to borrow it. It's a forward-moving force which has intent.

Making Space for Mothers’ Truths

These young women had put their own words to maternal ambivalence and had claimed it as their own. They truly get it. They exemplify the essence of my work, as I was given the opportunity to learn so much from their interactions and their wisdom.

I was watching my work being reimagined and retold through their own powerful voices and stories, which emphasized the importance of:

  • Accepting and normalizing what the everyday bag of mothering is filled with.
  • Being transparent about the feelings that you carry in your bag.
  • Engaging with the metaphor, which has the power to reach people—in this case, young mums who not only carry literal bags, but also emotional baggage with them.
  • Using technology to spread ideas and exchanges.
  • Providing a safe place for mums to talk, which helps to lift taboo and silence.
  • Having a supportive team around them.

They describe what motherhood means—"carrying a whole f****** bag of emotions." A real and raw summary of what we do as mums. Yet despite this, we can still move forward.

On their Instagram, they ask the question: “How have we never heard of maternal ambivalence?”

Now, their followers will.

item.title: When Understanding Yourself Isn’t Enough
item.description:
Defense Mechanisms

When Understanding Yourself Isn’t Enough

Sometimes knowing why we do something still isn't enough to change it.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • Understanding a pattern doesn't always lead to changing it.
  • Some of an individual's most established patterns were developed through experience, not explanation.
  • Sometimes, change needs a new experience—not just a better understanding of the old one.

I work with a lot of smart people.

And I’m not just saying that because I like to think that I must be smart if smart clients want to work with me. No, these are genuinely intelligent humans. They rapidly progressed in their careers and invented new ways to solve old problems. These are people who are used to figuring things out.

And it should come as no surprise that they apply the same rigor and logic to their work in the therapy room. They can tell you their attachment style, trace their childhood patterns into adulthood, and recognize when the part speaking is actually the voice of their parent. But that doesn’t always translate into change—and these brilliant folks get frustrated when they find that understanding themselves isn’t enough.

Not to knock understanding! As a species, we are meaning-makers. Whether it’s looking at the sky and writing myths to explain natural phenomena or obsessively solving today’s Wordle, we are wired to find patterns, solve puzzles, and understand the world around us. I’m just saying that understanding has its limits, especially when it comes to inner work.

I know that I need to relax more. I understand this deeply—I’ve read the research, spent my time in the client chair in therapy, and had my fair share of stress-related ailments. But when I find myself with a free afternoon, do I lay down and take a nap? No. Do I pick up that book I’ve been trying to finish for months and find myself a comfy chair? No. I worry about why my afternoon is free and what I’m forgetting. I think about how I should be spending my time, making lists to see what the best use of the afternoon will be. I chide myself for not having something already lined up that would help me relax and ensure I made the most of this. I understand the value of relaxing, and yet something in me just can’t.

Knowing isn't the same as experiencing

Now, here’s the part where I normally would try to explain to you why understanding doesn’t work and pull out some research to prove it. But honestly, that would just be me trying to get you to understand understanding. And that just doesn’t seem like a good use of anyone’s time.

Instead, I want you to think about a time when you felt something but didn’t understand it. Imagine you’re watching, binging your favorite show, and all of a sudden a scene comes out of nowhere and hits you like a ton of bricks. Maybe you feel warmth in your stomach, or your chest and throat start to tighten, and your eyes start to well up. And you have no idea why. There’s just something that touches you, moves something inside you, and allows you to feel deeply.

This is not new technology. For centuries, art has been allowing us to experience emotion without understanding it. Aristotle wrote about katharsis, the way that watching a tragic drama can evoke feelings in us and leave us changed. It’s not that the ancient Greeks invented somatic therapy, but they were on to something—we can be moved by something before we understand why. And I’m not saying everyone should quit therapy and go see a Broadway show (I like my job!), but I do think there’s some wisdom to learn here. We spend a lot of time up in the old cantaloupe (as a mentor of mine once said). And for some of us, that’s the only way we know how to be. But what would it be like to just feel things without needing to understand them?

The program was built for a reason

Sometimes, it feels like these patterns are long-running computer programs that desperately need an update. Some of mine have been running for a very long time. But it’s silly to think that 8-year-old Jaron was sitting around thinking, “Hmm. In order for me to avoid feeling pain, I think I’ll develop a cognitive schema that keeps me in the realm of understanding rather than risking me feeling something icky.” No, this process was likely rooted in the data that I had available to me at that age.

When I did well in school, I was praised. When I anticipated what someone wanted, I was shown affection. When I solved a problem, I didn’t feel helpless. When I understood why I didn’t get a part in the musical, it hurt less. And so I wove all those threads together and came up with a system designed to keep me praised, loved, in control, and out of pain. Insight didn’t build this—experience did. And if experience built these patterns, then I have a sense that new experience may be what starts to untangle them.

So, maybe the next time I find myself with a free afternoon, I’ll allow myself to indulge in a little experiment. Maybe I’ll sit down with my long-ignored book, and when that urge to make a “how to better use my free time” list comes up, I won’t run from it. I won’t try to figure out how to make the feeling go away. I’ll just experience it. And maybe my body will recognize that, uncomfortable though it may be, I am still ok. I am not less loved or deserving of praise because I didn’t figure out how to optimize my time.

Full disclosure, even now as I write, I can feel myself trying to figure out how to systematize this. Maybe that tells you how deep this program runs. But maybe the update doesn’t come from knowing the old software better. Maybe it comes from finally getting some new data.

item.title: The Limits of Communication Skills
item.description:
Relationships

The Limits of Communication Skills

Good communication begins before we speak.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • Good communication begins with becoming aware of what we're actually feeling inside.
  • Pausing helps us move beyond knee-jerk reactions and connect with more vulnerable feelings.
  • Sharing vulnerable feelings rather than blame can reduce defensiveness and deepen connection.
Source: pratsblog / Pixabay

As a psychotherapist for four decades, I’ve participated in my fair share of communication skills trainings—and I’ve learned a great deal from them. But I’ve noticed something vital that is often missing.

Many couples have entered my office wanting to improve their communication. I find that admirable. Communication—both verbal and non-verbal—is a bridge between two worlds, and the messages we send, whether intentional or not, can either connect us or distance us from each other.

Communication experts often emphasize the importance of using “I” statements. This means the emphasis is on what I am experiencing inside, versus the all-too-common “you” statements, which keep the focus on what the other person is doing wrong or how they can improve to meet our needs.

“You” statements often elicit defensiveness. For some odd reason (humor intended), people don’t like being told what we think is wrong with them. Such comments may elicit responses, whether verbalized or not, of:

  • Don’t criticize or judge me.
  • Don’t try to fix or change me.
  • Don’t scold me.
  • Don’t tell me what to do.

“You” statements often trigger shame—the painful sense that something’s wrong with us or that we possess some fundamental flaw. This shame can quickly escalate conflict. Shame is a common trigger for anger, which can become a way—conscious or not—of pushing our painful feelings back onto the other person.

He: You’re so messy. Why do you keep leaving dishes in the sink instead of putting them in the dishwasher?

She: You’re always so critical. You’re even messier than me. You’re always leaving your socks on the floor.

Such an exchange of criticisms and counter-accusations can damage the trust and intimacy a couple wants to build.

The Real Key to Communication

Learning the classic communication skills, such as using “I” statements, can certainly be helpful. But what often gets overlooked is that our communication is only effective to the extent that we’re aware of what we’re actually experiencing inside. It may seem simple enough to point out what we think is wrong with another person—if they could only see the light, everything would be fine!

Our hearts are more tender than we might recognize. Real or perceived criticisms tend to mix with the ways we already feel badly about ourselves. They may remind us of painful criticism from our past—creating the perfect storm for conflict to accelerate.

The key to effective communication—and deepening trust—is first becoming aware of what we’re actually experiencing inside. This means contacting the more vulnerable feelings that arise in us before speaking. What we’re often up against are automatic fight, flight, freeze, or appeasing responses. Something in us tries to protect us from emotional pain. We attack, shut down, or try to please and appease in order to maintain connection. While our inner protectors may succeed in reducing emotional discomfort in the short run, over time these automatic reactions can generate heartache and distance.

The Way Forward

A step forward is pausing long enough to drop down inside ourselves—sensing what we’re really feeling. Pausing gives us space to notice if there’s something tender we’re protecting—perhaps hurt, fear, embarrassment, or something else.

He: When I notice dishes in the sink, I feel irritated. And beneath that there’s a hurt place in me that feels like I’m left to take care of things by myself.

She: I didn’t realize that’s what it brought up for you. I can understand why you’d feel hurt. I’ll try to pay more attention.

Of course, she may not respond so gracefully, but we increase our chances of getting heard when we can courageously share what’s really happening inside us rather than succumbing to our knee-jerk reactions.

This kind of self-awareness and attuned communication is one expression of the power of gentle presence—listening inwardly before speaking outwardly, and sensing how best to do so. As I write in The Power of Gentle Presence:

“The greatest gift we can give another person is the gift of our own personal growth, self-awareness, and emotional honesty. The more we know ourselves and develop the courage and skills to communicate our authentic experience, the more that trust and love can flourish.”

Communication skills ultimately rest upon our capacity for self-awareness—and the gentle courage to share our true feelings and needs without attacking, blaming, or shaming the other person. One approach I find especially helpful is Focusing, based on research done by Eugene Gendlin and his colleagues at the University of Chicago. Focusing offers a process of slowing down, connecting with the feelings we’re noticing in our body, and hearing what they may be trying to tell us.

We can’t control the flow of love. But we can practice staying close to ourselves, which helps us feel closer to others. What we have the most control over is the ongoing practice of being gently present to what we’re actually experiencing and then communicating that—thereby creating a safer environment where love and intimacy are more likely to flourish.
